title: 1994 Pontiac Firebird SLP Firehawk Coupe: Bang for the Buck

body_markdown:
Though the fourth generation (1993–2002) of the Pontiac Firebird[was its last](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-gmmg-black-birds-were-a-fitting-sendoff-for-the-firebird/) , there was—and is—a lot to like. All the variants wore voluptuous and more aerodynamic styling, and buyers who wanted more oomph than the entry-level V-6 model had plenty to choose from, starting with the 275-hp, V-8-powered Formula and the similarly motivated[Trans Am](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/why-ill-never-sell-my-trans-am/) , with their additional amenities and extra swagger. For performance fans who had waited long enough for Detroit to produce a genuinely muscle-bound coupe, however, the star of the show was the SLP Firehawk.


A fine example of the breed is[up for auction on Hagerty Marketplace right now](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1994-Pontiac-Firebird/fcc7cfa0-7b41-47fa-a400-ed51cf91f818) , if you find yourself longing for an accessible, all-American performance car from the ’90s that’s quite uncommon. These special fourth-gen Firebirds were a collaboration between Street Legal Performance (SLP) and Pontiac—more accurately, the second iteration of a successful partnership. At the very tail end of the Firebird’s third generation, in 1991, Pontiac and SLP built 25 Firehawks (split between the ’91 and ’92 model years). In addition to an L98 V-8 modified to produce 360 hp, they boasted an extensive (and expensive) suite of upgrades geared toward enhancing their on-track performance, such as an aluminum driveshaft, the Corvette’s six-speed ZF manual, a Dana 44 rear end, Recaro seats, a roll bar, and stiffer rear control-arm bushings, plus optional (and even more expensive) Brembo brakes. The whole kit and kaboodle cost $51,989.

The 1993 iteration of the SLP Firehawk was not quite as extreme, and more approachable because of it. The ’93 Firehawk came with a 5.7-liter LT1 that made 300 hp at 5000 rpm and 330 at 2000 rpm. If you opted for the optional exhaust package, a 3-inch affair with a less restrictive muffler and dual tailpipes, those figures increased to 315 hp and 342 lb-ft. A six-speed manual came standard, and a four-speed automatic (as seen on our featured car) was optional. The price was far more accessible than that of its third-gen predecessor, with an MSRP below $25,000.


Hagerty Marketplace / Ohio.Corvettes.and.Musclecars


Though this isn’t a tiny car—the SLP Firehawk weighs in at 3476 pounds—the package was good for a 5.0-second zero-to-60-mph time as reported by *Car and Driver* in-period. As Pontiac triumphantly pointed out, that was quicker than the LT1-powered Chevrolet Corvette, the Nissan 300ZX Turbo, and the Ford Mustang Cobra. Plus, of all those cars, only the SLP Firehawk came standard with ABS and airbags for driver *and* passenger!


As the brochure proudly points out, because the SLP Firehawk was based on a Formula, all this performance was available with t-tops. Unfortunately, the car in the photos was not so equipped, but it does have the double distinction of a fairly early production number (#009 of about 504 produced for 1994) and an odometer reading of under 23,000 miles.

Thanks to the composite hood with its twin cold-air induction scoops, which aren’t just for show, the 17-inch five-spoke aluminum wheels, and the many *FIREHAWK* graphics, you wouldn’t have trouble identifying this as a Firehawk. Peek under the hood, and you’ll find just one subtle modification to the car, in the form of MSD ignition components. The stainless exhaust tips are another Firehawk-specific upgrade.


As of this writing, the example on Hagerty Marketplace has a high bid of $3000 with seven days left. That’s plenty of time to solidify your thoughts on what high-performance GM vehicle you’d like to be driving next summer!
